:::{#def-deviation}
#### Deviation

A **deviation** is the difference between a value and a reference value.
For any quantity $z$ and reference value $r$, the deviation of $z$ from $r$ is:

$$z - r$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

In probability and statistics,
"deviation" usually means deviation from a [population mean](expectation.qmd#def-expectation).

See: [Wikipedia: Deviation (statistics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deviation_(statistics))

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-deviation}
#### Deviation from a reference weight

A newborn weighing 3,200 g deviates from a reference weight of 3,500 g
by $3200 - 3500 = -300$ g.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-deviation-pop-mean}
#### Deviation from a population or subpopulation mean

The **deviation from the mean** of a random variable $Y$
is its [deviation](#def-deviation)
from its [expectation](expectation.qmd#def-expectation):

$$\devn(Y) \eqdef Y - \E{Y}$$

For a realized observation $y$:

$$\devn(y) \eqdef y - \E{Y}$$

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

Other sources often call this quantity an **error** or **noise term**.
In regression settings,
the reference mean is often conditional on covariates:
$\devn(y_i) \eqdef y_i - \E{Y_i \mid X_i = x_i}$.

These notes prefer "deviation"
for this mean-deviation quantity;
"error" and "noise" are common aliases.
The Morrison Lab's regression notes use "residual"
(defined in their [Linear regression chapter](https://morrison-lab.github.io/rme/chapters/Linear-models-overview.html#def-resid-fitted))
for deviations from fitted values,
write $\devn(\cdot)$ for these model/data deviations,
and reserve $\erf{\cdot}$ for estimator-to-estimand deviations
(see [Estimation](https://morrison-lab.github.io/rme/chapters/estimation.html#def-estimation-error)).

See:

- [Wikipedia: Errors and residuals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Errors_and_residuals)
- [Wikipedia: Deviation (statistics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deviation_(statistics))
- [Wikipedia: Linear regression --- Notation and terminology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_regression#Notation_and_terminology)

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-deviation-pop-mean}
#### Deviation of a die roll from its mean

A fair die roll $Y$ has $\E{Y} = 3.5$
(computed on the [expectation page](expectation.qmd#exm-linearity-expectation)),
so a roll of $y = 5$ has deviation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\devn(5) &= 5 - 3.5 \\
&= 1.5,
\end{aligned}
$$

and a roll of $y = 2$ has deviation

$$
\begin{aligned}
\devn(2) &= 2 - 3.5 \\
&= -1.5.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::
